standard.title: Equal Sharing and Grouping
standard.description: represent practical situations that involve equal sharing and grouping with physical and virtual materials and use counting or subitising strategies
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can quantify collections using counting and have experience with part-part-whole relationships to 10 (AC9MFN04). They have not yet applied the idea of equal groups — sharing so that each person gets the same amount, or forming groups of the same size.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students represent practical situations involving equal sharing and grouping using materials, and use counting or subitising to determine the size of equal groups.

nodes.label: The idea of equal
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify when a sharing situation is equal and when it is not, and explain what needs to happen to make it equal.
nodes.minimum_width: Distribute a small collection of objects between two groups and state whether the groups are equal, adjusting if they are not.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and create equal and unequal distributions; explain what makes sharing equal ('everyone has the same amount'); compare two groups using counting or subitising to check for equality.
wider: Explore equal sharing in familiar everyday contexts (fruit at snack time, cards dealt in a game) and discuss what equality means in each context
Investigate situations where objects cannot be shared equally (leftovers) — discussing what happens to the remainder at Foundation level

response_modes.reason: Students commonly conflate 'shared' with 'equal' — just distributing objects satisfies sharing in their view. Encountering varied sharing situations where equality is verified by checking each group helps students develop the precision of equal as same-amount-each.

nodes.hinge_reason: Nodes 2 and 3 both require students to verify equality of groups — which depends on understanding that equal means same-amount-each, not just distributed. Students who conflate shared with equal cannot confirm their distributions are valid or detect when grouping has produced unequal groups.
success_criteria: Student distributes a collection into equal groups and confirms each group has the same amount using counting or subitising
Student identifies an unequal distribution and adjusts it to make groups equal

nodes.label: Representing equal sharing situations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can represent a practical equal sharing situation using materials and find how many each person receives using counting or subitising.
nodes.minimum_width: Represent a sharing situation using materials (distribute a collection of up to 10 between 2 or 3 people) and count each group to find how many each person receives.
nodes.typical_width: Represent equal sharing situations across a range of practical contexts (fruit, cards, coins, beads); distribute collections of up to 10 objects between 2–4 people; use counting or subitising to determine the size of each equal group; confirm equality by comparing groups.
wider: Explore instructive games of First Nations Australians involving equal sharing — e.g. Yangamini of the Tiwi Peoples of Bathurst Island — investigating what makes sharing equal in a game context
Represent equal sharing using virtual materials or digital tools, comparing the process with physical sharing

response_modes.reason: The distribution process (one for you, one for me, one for you...) requires systematic allocation and tracking. Students commonly lose track or distribute unevenly. Repeated practice with the one-at-a-time distribution strategy builds the procedural fluency needed.

nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 (grouping contexts) requires students to form equal groups systematically — the same systematic allocation process as sharing. Students who cannot reliably execute the one-at-a-time distribution strategy cannot form equal groups of a specified size.
success_criteria: Student distributes a collection of up to 10 objects equally between 2–3 people using a systematic strategy
Student counts or subitises each group to confirm equal distribution and states how many each person received

nodes.label: Grouping contexts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can represent a practical grouping situation using materials, forming equal groups and counting or subitising to find the number in each group.
nodes.minimum_width: Form equal groups from a collection (e.g. put 6 objects into groups of 2) and count to verify the groups are equal.
nodes.typical_width: Represent equal grouping situations using materials; connect grouping to sharing as two forms of the equal-groups idea; use counting or subitising to find the number of groups or the number in each group; apply across varied practical contexts.
wider: Explore First Nations Australians' games that involve grouping or sharing, connecting the mathematical structure to cultural practice

Compare sharing (how many each) and grouping (how many groups) as different questions about the same situation — e.g. 'If I share 9 beads into groups of 3, how many groups do I get?' vs 'If I share 9 beads among 3 people, how many does each person get?'
Investigate what happens with collections that cannot be grouped evenly — identifying and counting the remainder

response_modes.reason: Students at Foundation see sharing and grouping as very different activities. Connecting them as two aspects of the equal-groups idea — through varied contexts where both questions arise — is the conceptual work that prepares students for multiplicative thinking in later years. Breadth across sharing and grouping contexts is what makes this connection visible.

Grouping integrates the equality concept (node 1) and sharing distribution process (node 2) into a new context. Students must apply the equal-groups idea in a direction that is less familiar (forming groups by size rather than distributing to people). The generalisation of equal groups is the integration point.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Connecting sharing and grouping as two faces of the same equal-groups idea is foundational for multiplicative reasoning. Advancing students who explore both and begin to see the relationship are engaging with genuinely deep mathematical thinking within the Foundation year band.
success_criteria: Student forms equal groups from a collection using materials and verifies equality by counting or subitising
Student can describe a grouping situation — naming the total, the group size, and the number of groups formed
